title: Why Is Printer Paper This Exact Shape? What We Know Today
parts: That sheet of paper? Fold an A4 sheet in half, and the halves keep the shape of the whole.
Fold again, and it still works. That is the shape's rule.
So why is printer paper this exact shape?
Wikipedia says ISO paper sizes share one aspect ratio. It is the square root of two, about one point four one four to one.
Our arithmetic: a square's diagonal is the square root of two times its side. So a sheet's long side matches the diagonal of a square on its short side.
Wikipedia says that ratio is unique: cut or fold the sheet in half, and the halves keep the same aspect ratio.
It adds that each next size is nearly exactly half the area of the prior size.
Our reading: one shape, many sizes. Fold a sheet, and you get the next size down.
Wikipedia says A0 is defined to have an area of one square meter.
It lists A4 as two hundred ten by two hundred ninety-seven millimeters.
Our arithmetic: A4 is four folds below A0, so sixteen A4 sheets cover about one square meter.
A Cambridge University page says one sheet of common A4 weighs five grams.
Where did the shape come from? Wikipedia says it was first mentioned in a letter written on October twenty-fifth, seventeen eighty-six.
The writer was a German physics professor, Lichtenberg.
A Cambridge translation says he planned to cut ordinary writing paper to the shape he wanted.
Then he found, with pleasure, that the paper already had that shape.
He wrote that the shape appeared not to have emerged by accident.
Wikipedia says Walter Porstmann argued in nineteen eighteen for basing paper formats on area.
A German national standard followed in the early nineteen twenties, say Wikipedia and Cambridge.
In nineteen seventy-five the format became an international standard, I S O two sixteen.
The Cambridge page adds that it also became the official United Nations document format that year.
Its main advantage, Wikipedia says, is scaling.
A copier can be designed to reduce a page from A4 to A5, or enlarge it from A4 to A3.
And an A4 sheet folded in half makes a brochure with A5 pages.
Wikipedia says the standard is used around the world except in North America, the Philippines, and parts of Latin America. We found no source that explains why.
Our reading: the shape is not a fashion. It is a rule that keeps every fold the same shape.
Our reading: when you fold a sheet, you handle a shape that already appears in a letter from seventeen eighty-six.
Some rules take years to agree. Others change in a single morning, after years of planning.
In nineteen sixty-seven, a whole country swapped sides of the road. Why?
